newsitem.title: JAPAN: ACCJ airs concerns about Japan insurance ratings.
newsitem.headline: ACCJ airs concerns about Japan insurance ratings.

text.p: The American Chamber of Commerce in Japan (ACCJ) on Wednesday urged Japan not to let an industry body set insurance premium rates and not to let authorities inhibit changes agreed on last year.

The ACCJ said in a statement that an industry rating body to be reorganised in line with last year's U.S.-Japan insurance agreement should issue purely advisory premium rates and have no role "either officially or unofficially" in setting rates.
Nor should the reorganised rating body be exempt from Japan's Anti-Monopoly law on even a limited basis, it added.

Under the 1996 bilateral agreement, Japan pledged to let insurers have different premium rates and to scrap a legal requirement that all insurers use rates set by the domestic industry's rating bodies.

Commenting on a report by a finance ministry advisory panel issued earlier this month, the ACCJ also expressed "serious reservations" about the panel's recommendations that government officials should keep some supervisory authority over the suitability of products and rates during a transition period.

"Such a supervisory role should be kept to a minimum, should be fair and transparent and should not be used as an excuse to maintain traditional regulatory approaches," the ACCJ said. "Most important, it should in no way inhibit the development of a sound, innovative market..."
The U.S. business group also urged the Japanese government to let foreign insurers become members of advisory panels to voice their views of deregulation of the sector.
